messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Raj, a meticulous 60-year-old hotel manager, had always prided himself on his unwavering composure, a trait essential in the demanding world of hospitality. But a year ago, an unforeseen catastrophe shattered that calm. While inspecting a newly installed industrial cleaning system in the hotel’s subterranean laundry facility, a pressure valve ruptured, unleashing a caustic cloud of concentrated disinfectant. Raj was engulfed, the acrid, metallic taste of the chemical instantly filling his mouth and burning his throat as he struggled to breathe. He remembered the blinding panic, the certainty that he was suffocating, dying, alone amidst the toxic fumes.

Since then, that horrifying moment has never truly left him. The acrid, metallic tang that had filled his mouth during the incident would suddenly return, sharp and immediate, even when he was tasting his morning coffee or supervising the kitchen staff. These vivid sensations were often the harbinger of an unwelcome intrusion: the memory would force its way into his mind, unwanted and unstoppable, feeling as though the event was happening right now, trapping him back in the suffocating plume. When he relived the event this way, his body would instantly respond, his muscles tensing, his heart pounding, his entire system on high alert. This constant physiological arousal, this feeling that his body was perpetually ready to react to danger, led him to believe that his body was fundamentally broken, unreliable.

This profound conviction that he could no longer trust his own body, coupled with a growing sense of helplessness that he couldn't stop bad things from happening, began to dictate his daily life. These negative appraisals fueled a constant vigilance. He started constantly checking his body for any unusual sensation – a slight cough, a faint metallic aftertaste, a dizzy spell – interpreting them as signs of residual damage or impending danger. His job, which once brought him satisfaction, became a minefield. He found himself meticulously scanning every room and corridor, especially in the service areas, for any unusual smells or signs of spills, his eyes darting, his posture rigid.

The persistent state of his body being on alert only intensified these maladaptive strategies, making him scan his surroundings even more compulsively, seeking an external threat to match his internal turmoil. Ironically, this constant body monitoring and environmental scanning kept his nervous system perpetually primed, maintaining the very state of alert he so desperately wanted to escape. He also noticed that when the intrusive memories struck, forcing him to relive the event, he would immediately heighten his vigilance, checking his pulse, his breathing, and the air around him, desperate to regain a sense of control.

His heightened state of threat also made the memories more frequent and intense. When his body felt constantly tense and ready to react, or when he reacted as if he was in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, the memory would more easily force its way into his mind, feeling more vivid and immediate. This cycle of memory and threat deeply reinforced his negative appraisals; each time he relived the event, it solidified his belief that he was helpless against these intrusions and that his own body was fundamentally unreliable.

Raj’s efforts to cope, however, often backfired. When colleagues or staff, oblivious to his struggles, would mention specific cleaning products, recent maintenance, or even the hotel’s emergency protocols, he would feel a surge of panic. He’d abruptly change the subject or find an excuse to leave the conversation, actively avoiding any reminders of the incident. This avoidance, while offering temporary relief, slowly isolated him, fostering a deep-seated belief that he no longer belonged anywhere, that he was fundamentally different from those around him who hadn't experienced what he had. This feeling of belonging nowhere and his overall helplessness were only compounded by his inability to stop these intrusive memories from occurring, making him feel even more at their mercy.

Furthermore, his constant vigilance and the false alarms that often accompanied them – such as assuming something bad was happening when a delivery was delayed – meant he was often reacting as if he was in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. This constant state of threat, in turn, fed his negative appraisals, reinforcing his conviction that his body was untrustworthy and that he was utterly helpless in the face of unseen dangers. The maladaptive strategies he employed, such as his constant checking, had unintended consequences: they kept his body on alert and paradoxically made him more prone to these false alarms, tightening the grip of his anxiety.

Lately, his relationship with his partner has grown strained due to his preoccupation and his increasing reluctance to socialize, especially if it involved public places or situations where he might be reminded of his vulnerability. He found himself unable to focus fully on his work, his mind constantly elsewhere, scanning for threats, lost in memories. Exhausted by the relentless cycle, Raj finally sought help. He came in, describing a life now dominated by an invisible, internal enemy, a silent chemical cloud that still lingered, leaving him desperate to find a way to trust his body again and escape the constant certainty that another bad thing was always just around the corner.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals -> Threat: The vignette does not convey that Raj's negative appraisals directly lead to a sense of threat or danger.
- Negative Appraisals -> Memory: The vignette does not convey that Raj's negative appraisals influence the nature or frequency of his intrusive memories.
- Maladaptive Strategies -> Memory: The vignette does not convey that Raj's maladaptive strategies directly influence the frequency or intensity of his intrusive memories.

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This profound conviction that he could no longer trust his own body, coupled with a growing sense of helplessness that he couldn't stop bad things from happening, began to dictate his daily life.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These deeply held beliefs made him feel constantly under threat, certain that danger lurked around every corner, both within his own body and in his environment.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When he relived the event this way, his body would instantly respond, his muscles tensing, his heart pounding, his entire system on high alert. This constant physiological arousal, this feeling that his body was perpetually ready to react to danger, led him to believe that his body was fundamentally broken, unreliable.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His conviction that he was so vulnerable, that his body was failing him, seemed to make the traumatic memory even more accessible and vivid, as if his mind was constantly replaying the evidence of his brokenness.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He started constantly checking his body for any unusual sensation – a slight cough, a faint metallic aftertaste, a dizzy spell – interpreting them as signs of residual damage or impending danger.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This constant vigilance, ironically, seemed to keep the traumatic memory fresh and easily triggered, as if his mind was searching for evidence to confirm his fears.
<<<END>>>
